§bmissionaries have been persistent in their efforts to spread their faith throughout§!

§b. Their strange beliefs and customs have caused much discussion and debate among our people. Now, they seek an audience with you, to present their case and ask for your acceptance of their god. Our ancestors have followed our traditional ways for countless generations, and our beliefs are deeply woven into the fabric of our society. Yet, the world around us is changing rapidly, and these foreigners bring with them promises of new knowledge, trade, and protection. Your advisors are divided on the matter. Some see opportunity in aligning with the foreigners' ways, hoping it will bring prosperity and shield us from the growing threats of colonial expansion. Others fear that accepting this new faith will erode our cultural identity and lead to the loss of our independence.§!
§bWord has reached us of a momentous occasion in§!
§b. The local ruler has embraced the teachings of our missionaries, accepting§!
§b. This joyous news heralds a new era of spiritual enlightenment and cooperation between our nations.§!
§b's conversion is a testament to the universal practicality of our beliefs and the dedication of our clergy abroad. May this be but the first of many such triumphs of faith in the South Pacific!§!

§bThe people in black robes who speak of their distant god have brought a curious gift to our land - tiny flying creatures they call 'honey bees'. These insects, we're told, were first carried here by the sister of one of their holy men. Now, another of these missionary folk has arrived, his hands full of humming boxes. This man, with his strange hat and smoky tool, visits our villages often. He shows us how to care for these buzzing strangers, speaking of the sweet gold they produce as if it were a blessing from his god. Some of our people are learning this new magic, tending to the singing boxes and harvesting the amber treasure within. The missionary has even written a book in§!

§b, to teach us more about these sky visitors. While these bees are not born of our earth, we are becoming skilled in their ways, wondering if this is another path to the sweetness their god promises.§!
§bFor the past year, our village has played host to a peculiar spectacle: a pale, oddly-dressed man who arrived with great fanfare from the land of §!

§b. This Reverend has been regularly gathering our people to listen to his amusing gibberish, which he delivers with great passion and many theatrical gestures. At first, we thought he might be touched in the head, but as the moons passed, we realized this was simply how the§!

§bcommunicate. Out of politeness and for some light entertainment, we've been pretending to understand his nonsensical ramblings. Some of the old woman have the trend of shouting "Amen!" whenever the funny man paused for breath, and soon it caught on. While the youth have developed an uncanny ability to mimic the Reverend's strange sounds, much to everyone's amusement. Little does the Reverend know, we've been placing bets on what he's actually trying to say. The most popular theories range from "The sky spirits demand more hats" to "Beware the uprising of the sentient yams."§!
§bIn a twist of fate that would make even the most stoic colonial administrator chuckle, our illustrious missionary has made a discovery of biblical proportions, in the far-flung islands of §!

§b. After a full year of what he believed to be soul-stirring sermons, tearful confessions, and miraculous conversions, the Reverend has come to the earth-shattering realization that he cannot, in fact, speak a single coherent word of the local language. It appears that the natives, in an act of either unprecedented politeness or a masterclass in deadpan comedy, have been nodding along to his linguistic gibberish with enthusiastic fervor. They've even gone so far as to punctuate his rambling monologues with well-timed "Amens," "Hallelujahs," and the occasional "Praise be!" in perfect§!
§b. Our colonial office is now faced with the delicate task of explaining to the Mission Society that their star converter has been preaching the gospel of complete nonsense.§!
§bOur humble village recently hosted a most intriguing guest from the lands of§!

§b. Clad in robes as pale as his skin, he introduced himself as a "missionary." We're not entirely sure what that means, but he certainly added flavor to our usually bland routines. During his stay, our village experienced a series of curious events. The fires burned with a strange new intensity, our cooking pots seemed more eager than usual to be filled, and everyone developed an inexplicable craving for exotic cuisine. Our guest's presence has stirred up quite an appetite for cultural exploration! Recognizing the rare opportunity before us, invited the visitor to partake in our most sacred feasts. When dawn broke, we found our guest had vanished, leaving nothing behind but a satisfied air and a few well-cleaned utensils. We can only assume he was eager to be taken in by other fortunate villages. Curiously, we all felt as if we'd incorporated a piece of him into ourselves - such is the power of cultural absorbtion!§!
§bOur noble quest to enlighten the far-flung corners of our empire has encountered a rather... unusual setback. A man of great faith and apparently delectable flavor, ventured into the wilds of§!

§bsome months ago. We regret to inform that he has, shall we say, become one with the local culture in a most unexpected manner. Initial reports from our perplexed colonial administrators suggested that the good Father's arrival coincided with a series of minor misfortunes—crops wilting, milk souring, and an inexplicable plague of mildly annoying insects. The superstitious locals, it seems, took this as a sign that our missionary would make a splendid main course at their next tribal gathering. Our search party, dispatched with utmost haste, returned with naught but a well-gnawed boot and a rather sheepish-looking tribal chief sporting a new set of robes suspiciously similar to the Father's Sunday best. When questioned, the chief merely burped and commented on the "divine flavor" of their recent feast. We must remember to be mindful of local customs—and perhaps invest in less appetizing missionaries.§!
